strategies.name: Sequential All-Reduce with In-Place Scaling
strategies.desc: Performs 16 dependent all-reduce operations sequentially, each preceded by in-place element-wise scaling (multiply by a[r]/W) and followed by in-place division (divide by a[r]). Results in 16 all-reduce dispatches with minimal memory overhead. Trades dispatch latency for memory efficiency and straightforward control flow.

strategies.name: Fused Scale-Reduce with Vectorized Operations
strategies.desc: Pre-computes all scaling factors and fuses the scale/divide operations into vectorized tensor operations before/after each all-reduce, eliminating per-shard loops where possible. Still requires 16 all-reduce dispatches but reduces local computation overhead by batching element-wise operations. Optimizes compute-to-communication ratio while maintaining the same collective count.

strategies.name: Pipelined All-Reduce with Double Buffering
strategies.desc: Uses two buffers to overlap computation (scaling/division of iteration i) with communication (all-reduce of iteration i-1) across the 16 iterations. Requires 16 all-reduce dispatches but hides local computation latency behind communication. Trades increased memory footprint (2x buffers) for reduced end-to-end walltime through pipeline parallelism.

strategies.name: Hierarchical Reduce-Scatter All-Gather Chain
strategies.desc: Decomposes each all-reduce into reduce-scatter followed by all-gather, enabling partial result computation on smaller chunks during the scatter phase. For 16 iterations, this yields 32 collective dispatches but each operates on 1/W of the data initially. Trades increased dispatch count for reduced per-dispatch payload size and better network utilization.

strategies.name: Batched Multi-Tensor All-Reduce
strategies.desc:
Groups multiple scale-reduce iterations into batched all-reduce calls where XLA runtime permits, concatenating scaled buffers across several iterations before dispatching. Reduces dispatch count from 16 toward ~4-8 by amortizing launch overhead across batches. Trades increased temporary memory allocation (batch concatenation) for fewer kernel launches and better hardware utilization.
